articles.title: Residential proxies detected on White House network
articles.summary: Residential proxies detected on White House network

top_comments: They’re too polite to say it explicitly, but when they say:> Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.There really aren’t very many candidates for who that person might be and it really seems like it would be someone who, I don’t know, maybe lives where the traffic is originating.
https://archive.ph/ado1HNot sure why the text is all black, but it's there

The danger here, of course, is that while these compromised devices are currently being monetized in a relatively benign way (other than bandwidth costs to the user, which to be sure can be nontrivial)… it would be naive to assume that there isn't a Command and Control capability that can assign less benign tasking - or can be compromised to do so.This also puts some of the troubling reports that politicians were bringing phones into SCIFs into context…

articles.title: A new Go API for JSON
articles.summary: A new Go API for JSON

top_comments: At this stage to me Go is the new C compiler. Quite honestly I spent 10 years or more writing Go code. At times 18 hours a day. And now with AI, I get models to write my Go code. I STILL want it to be Go code. Is that strange? No because I understand the performance and safety of Go. But I rarely write it directly anymore. Probably not at all in 6-9 months. Yet I still occasionally look at the code to see what the output looks like.So yea hopefully a nice new addition but only my prompts now matter. So need to make sure they pickup on the new API.
> "JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format [...]"Clearly it isn't, otherwise every language would have sorted it out by... a long time ago.

I generally like `encoding/json/v2` and I'm glad they did it.I wish they'd left `MarshalIndent` in there though. The equivalent code is super complicated and non-obvious, so it's a pain to migrate, and it's a pain when you're banging out some quick code and want to dump some readable JSON. I suppose these days the LLMs can write the complicated version for us, of course.

articles.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
articles.summary: Progress on provable inference for large language models

top_comments: This is built on VerInf, work that I did as a MARS fellow. They ripped everything down to the choice of 400B Maverick from us with very little attribution. Cool, I guess... https://github.com/jamespetrie/verinf

I've been writing about the need for provable inference (and training) on and off for a number of years; this is welcome news and a good start, and a significant improvement on prior zk results.The problems of inference proof for a closed model provider are more difficult than an open model provider -- you can get a probabilistic proof much more cheaply out of four independent inference providers running the same non-batched prompt than this 90-100x compute hit.Anthropic and others also have a significant problem with these proofs in that they have a lot of incentive internally to have some portions of the pre-prompt secret; I haven't read this newest scheme closely enough to determine if they have a way to hide parts of the prompt with the proof. But if they don't, they are almost certainly not going to want to send these proofs out in the general case.Last, I'll take this moment to soapbox and say for the researchers out there -- provable inference is nice. Provable training corpus information would be spectacular. It would be very, very, very nice to provide a set of model weights and a proof that they had only been trained on a dataset. To be clear, this is a really hard problem, but it would change fundamentally what levels of trust we could have about a given set of weights.

> In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers?> the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests, after which the provider has to commit again.> The client downloads the commitment, ~6.5 MB in all, and then one proof per request. Checking a proof takes 17 seconds on 24 threads (and 21 seconds on a single thread), including the offline phase's checkI know they mentioned $ETH in the technical report, but this is exactly the mechanic for a crypto currency Proof-of-Work which is expensive by design.When they announced it, I was hoping for a 5% overhead validation that the model that served you is really Fable and not Opus.The quantization bit caught me out, because we saw the boundary crossing from good-context-size to bad is so sharp it feels like longer context requests are sent to quantized models to make more room for more KV-Cache. This would expose those sorts of tricks people can play to have the same GPU do better on short context benchmarks and gracefully degrade on long context.At work, we did a bit of digging[1] into exactly why BaseTen, Fireworks and Together serve Inkling weights differently, we suspected the issue was a combination of how you do disaggregated prefill (+streaming) and quantization for longer context tasks.[1] - https://isotopes.ai/blog/everyone-is-selling-the-same-model-...

articles.title: Insects don't swarm at LED lights
articles.summary: Insects don't swarm at LED lights

top_comments: I have LED headlights and an LED light bar on my tractor and I can say with 100% confidence that bugs swarm both. To the point I have to wear glasses to keep them out of my eyes if I’m on it for more than about 30 seconds at night.I’m guessing he’s confusing the dramatic drop in insect life overall with a change in behavior due to different lights.

Welp, they do for mine. I've had to stop turning on outdoor LEDs because angry bees kept showing up, and there'd be 3-10 dead ones on my doorstep every morning. These are white bulbs. Might be "zombees."Also, not sure about white bulbs, but those color-configurable spotlights definitely emit UV at least when set to anything near blue/purple. They cause certain things to glow. Probably white is doing it too but it's harder to see.

My pet theory is that the dimmable LEDs repel insects (when used as a grow light).The thing that insects can see and we don't is the rapid flashing of a PWM power controller.I wonder if these streetlights have power saving fade-ins as the nightfall approaches instead of clicking on at sunset.Like - https://doi.org/10.1109/CSNT51715.2021.9509652
